Purpose

This file consolidates the project documentation related to FIRO and The Human Element into a single knowledge-base chapter in Quarto format.

Note on terminology: the request referred to “FIFO and Human Element”. In this context, the intended term is almost certainly FIRO, which is the interpersonal theory developed by Will Schutz and later extended into The Human Element.

Executive overview

The Human Element is a personal and interpersonal development framework created by Will Schutz. It focuses on how awareness, choice, truthfulness, self-esteem, and behavioural flexibility affect performance, relationships, leadership, trust, and team effectiveness.

A central intellectual foundation beneath The Human Element is FIRO:

  • Fundamental
  • Interpersonal
  • Relations
  • Orientation

FIRO explains interpersonal behaviour through recurring human needs and concerns that appear in relationships, teams, and organisations. In its widely used form, it focuses on three dimensions:

  1. Inclusion
  2. Control
  3. Openness / Affection

Within the broader Human Element tradition, these dimensions are often interpreted not only as behavioural patterns, but also as gateways to deeper issues of belonging, competence, authenticity, trust, and self-regard.

Why this matters

For leadership, team performance, coaching, facilitation, project delivery, and organisational change, technical competence is often not enough. Teams can fail despite strong technical capability because of:

  • unspoken tension
  • low trust
  • defensive behaviour
  • fear of conflict
  • lack of psychological safety
  • hidden needs for inclusion, control, or closeness
  • poor emotional transparency
  • unresolved status or authority struggles

The Human Element addresses these hidden human dynamics directly.

Origins and background

Will Schutz

Will Schutz was a psychologist whose work began with research into group compatibility and interpersonal behaviour. His early work developed into FIRO, and later into The Human Element, which integrated interpersonal theory with a broader developmental and experiential methodology.

From FIRO to The Human Element

A useful way to understand the evolution is:

  • FIRO began as a theory of interpersonal behaviour
  • FIRO-B became a behavioural instrument to assess interpersonal preferences and patterns
  • The Human Element expanded the model into a fuller developmental system involving self-awareness, emotional honesty, choice, self-esteem, and group effectiveness

This progression matters because it shows that The Human Element is not merely a personality questionnaire. It is an approach to human effectiveness that combines:

  • theory
  • self-inquiry
  • reflection
  • emotional awareness
  • experiential learning
  • group process work
  • application to leadership and organisations

Core structure of FIRO

The three dimensions

Inclusion

Inclusion relates to contact, visibility, participation, recognition, belonging, and whether a person feels “in” or “out”.

Common questions beneath inclusion include:

  • Do I belong here?
  • Am I seen?
  • Am I accepted?
  • Do I matter to this group?
  • How much contact do I want with others?

Typical team expressions:

  • joining or withdrawing
  • speaking up or staying silent
  • seeking attention or avoiding exposure
  • wanting frequent interaction or preferring distance
  • feeling excluded, overlooked, or unnecessary

At work, inclusion often appears in:

  • onboarding
  • team meetings
  • participation in decisions
  • stakeholder engagement
  • social integration
  • workshop dynamics
  • cross-functional collaboration

Control

Control relates to influence, responsibility, structure, power, authority, competence, and decision rights.

Common questions beneath control include:

  • Am I competent?
  • Who decides?
  • How much influence do I have?
  • Can I trust others to lead or deliver?
  • Do I need structure or freedom?

Typical team expressions:

  • directing vs following
  • organising vs resisting direction
  • ambiguity tolerance
  • conflict over ownership
  • micro-management
  • struggle over accountability
  • preference for clear governance vs flexible autonomy

At work, control often appears in:

  • decision-making forums
  • governance structures
  • delegation
  • accountability
  • role clarity
  • escalation paths
  • programme and project leadership

Openness / Affection

In classic FIRO language this dimension was often called Affection. In later Human Element and related interpretations it is frequently rendered as Openness, emphasising authenticity, emotional transparency, closeness, warmth, and trust.

Common questions beneath openness include:

  • Can I be real here?
  • Am I liked?
  • Can I trust this person?
  • Is it safe to tell the truth?
  • How much emotional closeness do I want?

Typical team expressions:

  • honesty vs guardedness
  • warmth vs distance
  • trust vs suspicion
  • empathy vs detachment
  • emotional disclosure vs emotional control
  • direct feedback vs polite avoidance

At work, openness often appears in:

  • feedback conversations
  • conflict resolution
  • mentoring
  • leadership presence
  • one-to-ones
  • trust building
  • collaboration under pressure

Expressed and wanted behaviour

A very practical element in FIRO-based work is the difference between what a person expresses toward others and what the person wants from others.

Examples:

  • Someone may express high inclusion by inviting others in, yet want low inclusion and still feel crowded.
  • Someone may express low control but want high control, creating frustration.
  • Someone may express warmth but want little openness in return, or the reverse.

This distinction is useful because many interpersonal tensions arise not from one trait alone, but from the mismatch between:

  • what I do
  • what I want
  • what others do
  • what others want

Human Element principles

The Human Element extends beyond behavioural preference into deeper developmental work.

Awareness

Awareness means noticing what is happening in oneself and in the group:

  • feelings
  • assumptions
  • bodily signals
  • reactions
  • defensiveness
  • stories we are telling ourselves
  • the impact we have on others

Without awareness, people act automatically and often defensively.

Choice

One of the strongest Human Element ideas is that people often feel they “have no choice” when in fact they do have choice, even if the available choices are difficult.

Growth comes from recognising:

  • what I am doing
  • why I am doing it
  • what alternatives I have
  • what consequences follow from each option

Truthfulness

Truthfulness does not mean brutal honesty or emotional dumping. It means reducing distortion and becoming more real, more congruent, and less defended.

In practice this can mean:

  • naming what is happening
  • acknowledging discomfort
  • speaking clearly about needs and boundaries
  • giving feedback honestly and respectfully
  • reducing pretence

Self-esteem

A defining Human Element view is that many performance and relationship problems are rooted in impaired self-esteem.

Low self-esteem may show up as:

  • defensiveness
  • control behaviour
  • perfectionism
  • withdrawal
  • blame
  • avoidance
  • over-compliance
  • status anxiety
  • inability to receive feedback

Healthy self-esteem supports:

  • openness
  • accountability
  • curiosity
  • resilience
  • confidence without domination
  • connection without dependency

Congruence

Congruence is alignment between:

  • what I feel
  • what I think
  • what I say
  • what I do

The more congruent a person is, the more trustworthy and effective they tend to be.

The Human Element in groups and organisations

Group effectiveness

The Human Element suggests that group performance depends not only on technical capability, but also on the quality of interpersonal relations.

A technically strong team may still underperform because of:

  • hidden agendas
  • fear of embarrassment
  • lack of trust
  • superficial agreement
  • dependence on hierarchy
  • unresolved authority issues
  • silence around conflict
  • low willingness to say what is true

Leadership

For leaders, the model is particularly useful because it highlights the hidden emotional and relational layers under everyday management problems.

Examples:

Inclusion-related leadership issues

  • people not speaking in meetings
  • stakeholders feeling left out
  • cliques within teams
  • remote staff becoming invisible
  • new joiners struggling to integrate

Control-related leadership issues

  • unclear authority
  • duplication of decisions
  • micro-management
  • passive resistance
  • confusion over ownership
  • weak escalation discipline

Openness-related leadership issues

  • lack of trust
  • conflict avoidance
  • performative agreement
  • guarded communication
  • poor quality feedback
  • inability to discuss difficult topics

Change and transformation

During change, Human Element work helps explain why resistance is often emotional and relational rather than purely rational.

People may resist because they fear:

  • exclusion
  • loss of competence
  • loss of control
  • loss of identity
  • loss of status
  • loss of relationship security

That makes the framework useful in:

  • organisation design
  • programme leadership
  • transformation offices
  • mergers
  • leadership transitions
  • team reset workshops
  • post-conflict repair

Practical interpretation of the three dimensions

Inclusion in practice

Healthy inclusion tends to look like:

  • balanced participation
  • clear welcome
  • people feeling seen
  • appropriate involvement
  • respectful visibility

Dysfunctional inclusion patterns can include:

  • isolation
  • attention-seeking
  • social over-dependence
  • disengagement
  • chronic exclusion
  • token involvement

Questions for reflection:

  • Who feels included in this team?
  • Who is consistently left out?
  • Who dominates airtime?
  • Who never volunteers?
  • Where are people seeking recognition indirectly?

Control in practice

Healthy control tends to look like:

  • clear accountability
  • proportionate authority
  • good delegation
  • confidence with boundaries
  • structured freedom

Dysfunctional control patterns can include:

  • power struggle
  • over-control
  • abdication
  • dependency
  • ambiguity
  • hidden vetoes
  • passive resistance

Questions for reflection:

  • Who really decides here?
  • Is accountability explicit?
  • Are people over-directed or under-led?
  • Where does ownership break down?
  • Where is authority assumed but not agreed?

Openness in practice

Healthy openness tends to look like:

  • honesty
  • warmth
  • trust
  • empathy
  • appropriate vulnerability
  • respectful candour

Dysfunctional openness patterns can include:

  • guardedness
  • emotional distance
  • pseudo-harmony
  • gossip
  • avoidance
  • overexposure without containment

Questions for reflection:

  • Can people tell the truth here?
  • What remains unsaid?
  • Is feedback safe?
  • Are relationships real or performative?
  • Is conflict handled directly?

Common Human Element workshop themes

A Human Element workshop or facilitation intervention may include themes such as:

  • self-awareness
  • self-esteem
  • choice and responsibility
  • interpersonal impact
  • inclusion, control, and openness
  • defensive routines
  • emotional literacy
  • truthfulness and candour
  • team trust
  • conflict and feedback
  • leadership presence
  • psychological safety
  • alignment between intention and impact

Activities may involve:

  • self-reflection
  • paired dialogue
  • group exercises
  • structured feedback
  • experiential activities
  • discussion of real work situations
  • facilitated exploration of assumptions and emotions

Links to FIRO-B and related instruments

The FIRO tradition includes formal instruments such as FIRO-B and later related measures. These can be useful when used responsibly, especially in:

  • coaching
  • team development
  • leadership development
  • workshop facilitation
  • relationship awareness
  • conflict analysis

However, in practical organisational use, the value is not only in the score. The value comes from the conversation around:

  • patterns
  • needs
  • reactions
  • mismatches
  • blind spots
  • choices for change

Application in project, programme, and PMO contexts

Because this project often explores leadership, governance, consulting, PMO, and stakeholder dynamics, the Human Element can be applied directly.

Stakeholder engagement

FIRO provides a useful lens for stakeholder behaviour:

  • some stakeholders want high inclusion and regular contact
  • some want high control and strong decision rights
  • some value openness and trust before they commit
  • some become disruptive when their core needs are frustrated

Questions to ask:

  • Does this stakeholder need visibility, influence, reassurance, trust, or autonomy?
  • Are they reacting to the content of the work, or to how they are being engaged?
  • Is their resistance really about the proposal, or about belonging, power, or safety?

Project governance

Many governance issues that appear procedural are partly interpersonal:

  • steering committees that do not make decisions
  • sponsors who overrule informally
  • teams that hide bad news
  • workstreams that compete for authority
  • delivery teams that feel excluded from decisions

Human Element interpretation:

  • Inclusion: who is invited into the conversation?
  • Control: who believes they have the right to decide?
  • Openness: who feels safe enough to tell the truth?

PMO leadership

A PMO can use the Human Element in:

  • workshop design
  • stakeholder analysis
  • conflict repair
  • escalation coaching
  • retrospectives
  • leadership diagnostics
  • team reset interventions
  • role and governance clarity work

Relationship to psychological safety

The Human Element overlaps with the modern concept of psychological safety, but it is not identical.

Psychological safety usually focuses on whether people feel safe to speak up, ask questions, admit mistakes, and contribute.

The Human Element goes further by exploring:

  • self-esteem
  • authenticity
  • defensive behaviour
  • truthfulness
  • relational needs
  • the emotional roots of silence, control, and conflict

In this sense, psychological safety can be seen as compatible with Human Element practice, while Human Element offers deeper language for what may be happening beneath the surface.

Strengths of the Human Element approach

Strengths

  • practical and human-centred
  • useful for teams, leadership, and relationships
  • explains recurring interpersonal tension clearly
  • integrates behaviour with deeper self-awareness
  • applicable in coaching, facilitation, and organisational development
  • helps connect performance problems with relational dynamics
  • highly relevant where trust and candour matter

Typical value

  • improved communication
  • better conflict handling
  • stronger trust
  • more honest feedback
  • reduced defensiveness
  • clearer leadership behaviour
  • stronger team cohesion
  • better decision quality

Limitations and cautions

The framework is powerful, but it should be used carefully.

Cautions

  • It is not a substitute for clinical or therapeutic treatment.
  • It should not be used to label or trap people.
  • Assessment scores should be interpreted with care.
  • Deep emotional work requires skilled facilitation.
  • Cultural context matters.
  • Organisational problems are not only interpersonal; structure, incentives, workload, and strategy also matter.

A weak application turns the model into simplistic typing. A strong application uses it as a lens for dialogue, awareness, and responsible choice.

Suggested facilitation questions

Individual reflection

  • When do I feel most included?
  • When do I feel ignored or marginalised?
  • How do I react when I lack control?
  • How do I behave when I feel incompetent?
  • What makes it hard for me to be open?
  • What truths do I avoid saying?
  • What defensive pattern do I return to under stress?

Team reflection

  • What do we avoid talking about?
  • Where is trust high and low?
  • Who is not really included?
  • How clear are decision rights?
  • What happens when conflict appears?
  • Do people feel safe enough to say bad news early?
  • What would more truthfulness look like in this team?

Leadership reflection

  • Do I create inclusion or dependency?
  • Do I provide clarity or over-control?
  • Do I invite candour or shut it down?
  • Can people disagree with me safely?
  • What human need is driving the resistance I see?

A concise working model

A simple working model for practitioners is:

  1. Notice behaviour
  2. Identify the interpersonal dimension
    • inclusion
    • control
    • openness
  3. Explore underlying fear or need
  4. Increase awareness
  5. Create real choice
  6. Encourage truthful dialogue
  7. Support responsibility and self-esteem
  8. Translate insight into new behaviour
